_note: English idioms and proverbs (/knowledge/idioms), B1–C1, British English. idioms-mistakes run (2026-10-30), status entwurf per entry. Field names stay German: de = the English idiom, bild = the literal picture, bedeutung = the meaning, bsp = examples, wann = when people say it, en = a plain-English paraphrase, herkunft = origin. An origin is told only where Wiktionary's etymology (checked 2026-10-30) supports it; everything else says the origin is unknown. scripts/check-redewendungen.mjs checks the format.

tipp.say: Cats and dogs from the sky? Where?
A piece of cake? Yes, please!
An arm and a leg? Too expensive!

eintraege.bild: Cats and dogs are falling from the sky.
eintraege.bedeutung: It is raining very hard.
bsp: Take an umbrella – it's raining cats and dogs!
It rained cats and dogs all weekend, so we stayed in.
eintraege.wann: When the rain is very heavy. A bit old-fashioned, but everyone knows it.

herkunft.text: Nobody knows for sure. We found no reliable source that explains where it comes from, so we don't tell a story here.

comic.quaki: Quaki looks up and sees cats and dogs falling out of the clouds.

eintraege.de: let the cat out of the bag
eintraege.bild: Someone opens a bag, and a cat jumps out.
eintraege.bedeutung: to tell a secret, often by mistake
bsp: We planned a surprise party, but Tom let the cat out of the bag.
Don't let the cat out of the bag – it's a secret!
eintraege.wann: When someone tells a secret that should stay secret, often without meaning to.

herkunft.text: First recorded in the middle of the 18th century. The usual explanation: it is the opposite of buying “a pig in a poke” (a pig in a bag). If a dishonest trader put a cat in the bag instead of a pig and the cat got out, the trick was discovered.

comic.quaki: Quaki opens a shopping bag and a cat jumps out.

eintraege.de: take something with a pinch of salt

herkunft.text: The form with a grain of salt is often traced to Latin cum grano salis and to the Roman writer Pliny, who tells of an antidote to poison taken with a grain of salt. This is repeated a lot, but it is not well proven.

eintraege.bild: A whole book fits inside a nutshell.

herkunft.text: It comes from Latin in nuce (in a nut). The Roman writer Pliny the Elder tells that Cicero once saw the whole Iliad, a very long poem, written on parchment so small that it fitted into a nutshell.

eintraege.de: The early bird catches the worm.
eintraege.bild: A bird catches a worm at sunrise.
eintraege.bedeutung: People who start early have the best chances.
bsp: Get to the sale at eight – the early bird catches the worm.
She's always first in the office. The early bird catches the worm!
eintraege.wann: To encourage someone to start early. An early bird is a person who gets up early.
eintraege.en: If you start early, you succeed.

herkunft.text: Nobody knows for sure. We found no reliable source that explains where it comes from, so we don't tell a story here.

eintraege.de: There's no point crying over spilt milk.
eintraege.bild: Someone cries next to a glass of milk on the floor.
eintraege.bedeutung: Don't be upset about something that has happened and can't be changed.
bsp: You missed the train, but there's no point crying over spilt milk.
It's done now – no point crying over spilt milk.
eintraege.wann: To comfort someone after a small mistake or loss. Also: It's no use crying over spilt milk.
eintraege.en: Don't worry about what you can't change.

herkunft.text: Nobody knows for sure. We found no reliable source that explains where it comes from, so we don't tell a story here.

comic.quaki: Quaki looks sadly at a glass of milk on the floor.

eintraege.de: Every cloud has a silver lining.
eintraege.bild: A dark cloud with a shining silver edge.
eintraege.bedeutung: There is something good in every bad situation.
bsp: I lost my job, but every cloud has a silver lining: now I can retrain.
Every cloud has a silver lining – the delay gave us time to talk.
eintraege.wann: To comfort someone after bad news.
eintraege.en: Something good comes out of everything.

herkunft.text: The silver lining goes back to John Milton's poem Comus (1634), in which a dark cloud turns its silver lining towards the night. The proverb came later and refers to this picture.

comic.quaki: Quaki points at the bright edge of a dark cloud.

eintraege.bild: One person helps while another only talks.
eintraege.bedeutung: What you do matters more than what you say.
bsp: He says he'll help, but actions speak louder than words.
Don't promise – show me. Actions speak louder than words.
eintraege.wann: When someone promises a lot but does little.
eintraege.en: Doing is more important than saying.

herkunft.text: Nobody knows for sure. We found no reliable source that explains where it comes from, so we don't tell a story here.

eintraege.de: Don't judge a book by its cover.
eintraege.bild: A book with an ugly cover has a wonderful story inside.
eintraege.bedeutung: Don't decide what someone or something is like only from how they look.
bsp: The café looks old, but don't judge a book by its cover – the food is great.
Don't judge a book by its cover: he's actually very kind.
eintraege.wann: When someone judges a person or a place too quickly.

herkunft.text: Nobody knows for sure. We found no reliable source that explains where it comes from, so we don't tell a story here.

eintraege.de: Rome wasn't built in a day.
eintraege.bild: Builders work on a huge city – it takes years.
eintraege.bedeutung: Big things take time.
bsp: Learning a language takes time – Rome wasn't built in a day.
Be patient with the garden. Rome wasn't built in a day!
eintraege.wann: To tell someone to be patient.

herkunft.text: Probably a translation of an old French proverb, Rome ne fut pas faite toute en un jour (Rome was not made all in one day).

comic.quaki: Quaki builds a tiny Rome out of bricks, one by one.

eintraege.de: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
eintraege.bild: Ten cooks put salt into one pot of soup.
eintraege.bedeutung: If too many people work on the same thing, the result is bad.
bsp: Let's have just two people plan the party – too many cooks spoil the broth.
Everyone changed the text, and too many cooks spoiled the broth.
eintraege.wann: When too many people want to decide.
eintraege.en: Too many helpers make things worse.

eintraege.de: Where there's a will, there's a way.
eintraege.bild: Someone climbs over a high wall to reach the other side.
eintraege.bedeutung: If you really want something, you will find a way to do it.
bsp: She had no money for university, but where there's a will, there's a way.
We'll finish on time – where there's a will, there's a way!
eintraege.wann: To encourage someone with a difficult goal.

eintraege.bild: Someone is sweating at the gym.
eintraege.bedeutung: You have to work hard, or suffer a bit, to achieve something.
bsp: My legs hurt after the run, but no pain, no gain!
No pain, no gain – one more exercise!
eintraege.wann: Mostly about sport and hard training. Informal.

eintraege.de: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
eintraege.bild: A visitor in Rome eats and dresses like the people there.
eintraege.bedeutung: When you are in another place, follow the customs of the people there.
bsp: In Japan we took our shoes off – when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
Everyone eats late here. When in Rome!
eintraege.wann: When you travel or live abroad. Often shortened to: When in Rome!

herkunft.text: The oldest form is a Latin saying linked to St Ambrose, a bishop of Milan in the 4th century: if you are in Rome, live in the Roman way. In English it is recorded in the early 1600s.

comic.quaki: Quaki eats pasta in Rome, like everyone around him.
